title: Founder case: Ben & Jerry's starts small

sources.claim: Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield took a $5 correspondence course in ice cream making from Penn State and opened their first shop in a renovated gas station in Burlington, Vermont, in 1978; they had first considered bagels but found the equipment too expensive.

sections.skill: Apply a documented early decision: learn cheaply, start small

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how did the founders learn ice cream making?

choices.text: Buying an existing ice cream company
Working several years in a big ice cream factory first
A degree in food science
A low-cost correspondence course from Penn State

questions.correct_answer: A low-cost correspondence course from Penn State
questions.intro: Documented history: Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield took a $5 correspondence (mail) course in ice cream making from Penn State. In 1978 they opened their first scoop shop in a renovated gas station in Burlington, Vermont. They had first thought about bagels, but the equipment cost too much. Lesson drawn by this course (an interpretation, not their words): learn the skill cheaply, pick an idea whose start-up costs you can afford, and begin with one small location. One success story does not guarantee the same result for another business.
questions.feedback: The documented history says they took a $5 correspondence course.

questions.intro: A good lesson from a founder story uses what is documented, such as a course taken, a first location, or a choice between two ideas. Enthusiasm is different: a friend saying "your shop will be amazing" is a feeling, not evidence. When you study a case, separate the facts that are recorded from the hopes and from later success. Later fame does not prove that each early step was the reason; it only shows what happened in that case.
